arable

/AIR-uh-buhl/ - rhymes with parable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Arable means suitable for growing crops.

Less than a tenth of the mountain kingdom is arable, so every scrap of level ground has been terraced and planted for centuries.

Example

In 1940 the ministry sent surveyors out with one question: what else can be plowed? Golf links, deer parks, village greens — each was walked, augered, and judged. Good depth of soil, drainage, a slope a tractor could hold: onto the list it went, and by spring the fairways were under wheat. The blockade had turned a lazy word on old maps into the most urgent question in the country.

Arable is the exact word for what those surveyors were hunting, because it means suitable for growing crops — nothing more and nothing less. It does not promise a good yield, and it says nothing about beauty or ownership; it draws the one line that mattered that year, between ground that can feed people and ground that cannot.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

farmable: Farmable is the plain, everyday way to say it: this ground can be farmed. Arable is the surveyor's and geographer's term for the same judgment — land suitable for growing crops — the word that maps, ministries, and land registries reach for.

plowable: Plowable makes a narrower claim than arable: the blade can cut this ground, and that is all. Arable adds the judgment that matters — soil deep and sound enough for crops to grow once the plowing is done. A gravel flat may be plowable yet never arable.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

untillable: ground no plow can even enter — rock, bog, or slope

sterile: ground where nothing can take root at all

Where it sits · how much the soil can yield — barren → arable → bountiful

barren vs. arable: Barren ground sits at the floor of this scale, far below arable: it answers every seed the same way — with nothing — while arable land can at least be plowed and planted.

bountiful vs. arable: Bountiful goes past arable — arable only promises that crops can grow; bountiful means the ground is already pouring out more than its people can store.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ar-

Root — ar-: to plow (Latin arare)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Ar- (to plow) + -able (able to be) = able to be plowed. Latin arare was the everyday verb for driving a plow through the ground, and arable land is literally land that will take the blade — the oldest test of whether a place can feed its people.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Arable is the last common English trace of Latin arare, "to plow." The verb itself never made the crossing into English — even plow comes from a different, Germanic line — so arable stands alone, one word carrying a whole lost verb on its back.

Strength Check

Word Choice

technical / geographic

Arable is the surveyor's and geographer's word — arable land, arable acreage — and it draws a hard line: can crops grow here or not? It says nothing about how much will grow; for that, reach for fertile or bountiful. Keep it apart from this unit's agrarian, which describes societies: a nation can be short of arable land and still be thoroughly agrarian in how it lives.
